title: Hashing, Checksums and Bloom Filters
summary: You will understand hash functions and collisions (with birthday-paradox math), checksums vs cryptographic hashes, and how Bloom filters and HyperLogLog trade a little accuracy for huge memory savings.

questions.prompt: What is a hash function, and what properties make a good one for a hash table? Why are collisions unavoidable?
questions.hint: Inputs can be any size; outputs are a fixed size.
keyPoints: A hash function maps input of any size to a fixed-size value (e.g. 32 or 64 bits).
Good properties: deterministic, fast, uniform distribution over outputs, avalanche (small input change flips ~half the output bits).
Collisions are unavoidable by the pigeonhole principle: there are more possible inputs than outputs.
Hash tables handle collisions (e.g. chaining or open addressing); uniformity keeps them rare and lookups O(1) on average.
questions.answer:
A **hash function** takes input of any size (a word, a 2 GB file) and returns a **fixed-size** number, e.g. 32 or 64 bits.

Properties of a good one for a hash table:

- **Deterministic:** same input, same output, every time.
- **Fast:** it runs on every lookup.
- **Uniform:** outputs are spread evenly over all buckets, so no bucket gets crowded.
- **Avalanche effect:** changing one input bit flips about half the output bits, so similar keys (`user1`, `user2`) land far apart.

**Collisions are unavoidable** because of the **pigeonhole principle**: there are infinitely many possible inputs but only 2^32 (or 2^64) outputs, so some different inputs *must* share a hash. With buckets it's even more obvious: 1,000 keys into 100 buckets.

Hash tables handle collisions with **chaining** (each bucket holds a small list) or **open addressing** (probe the next free slot). A uniform hash keeps those lists short, so lookups stay **O(1) on average**.

questions.prompt: A service gives each new user a **random 32-bit ID** (no uniqueness check). After **100,000** users, what is the probability that at least two share an ID? About how many users until it reaches 50%? What would you use instead?
keyPoints: P ≈ 1 − e^(−1.16) ≈ 0.69, about a 69% chance of a collision.
Use 64-bit (or larger, e.g. UUID/128-bit) IDs, a database sequence, or a Snowflake-style generator; and/or enforce a unique constraint.

questions.prompt: Compare **CRC32**, **SHA-256**, **HMAC-SHA256** and **bcrypt**. For each, say what it protects against and give one place it is used.
questions.hint: Accidents vs attackers; anyone can compute vs needs a secret; fast vs deliberately slow.
keyPoints: CRC32: detects accidental corruption (bit flips, bursts up to 32 bits); used in Ethernet, ZIP, PNG; not secure, attackers can forge matching data.
SHA-256: cryptographic hash, preimage and collision resistant; used for file integrity, Git-style content addressing, certificates/signatures.
HMAC-SHA256: hash combined with a secret key, proves authenticity and integrity; used to sign webhooks and API requests.
bcrypt (or scrypt/argon2): deliberately slow, salted password hashing to resist brute force; SHA-256 is too fast for passwords.
Mentions MD5/SHA-1 are broken for security (practical collisions).
questions.answer:
| | Protects against | Where it's used |
|---|---|---|
| **CRC32** | **Accidental** corruption: random bit flips and burst errors up to 32 bits | Ethernet frames, ZIP and PNG files |
| **SHA-256** | Tampering you can detect by comparing to a trusted hash: preimage resistant (can't find an input for a hash) and collision resistant (can't find two inputs with the same hash) | Verifying downloads, content addressing (Git-style IDs), certificates and digital signatures |
| **HMAC-SHA256** | Forgery: hash + a **secret key**, so only someone with the key can produce a valid tag. Proves **authenticity and integrity** | Signing webhooks (e.g. Stripe, GitHub), signing API requests |
| **bcrypt** (or scrypt/argon2) | Brute-forcing stolen password hashes: **salted** and deliberately **slow** (e.g. ~100 ms per guess) | Storing user passwords |

Key distinctions:

- **CRC32 is not secure:** an attacker can easily change data and fix up the checksum to match.
- **SHA-256 is too fast for passwords:** a GPU can try billions per second, so a leaked database of SHA-256 passwords gets cracked quickly. bcrypt makes each guess expensive.
- Anyone can compute SHA-256; only key holders can compute an HMAC.
- **MD5 and SHA-1 are broken** for security: practical collisions have been found, so use SHA-256 or better.

questions.prompt: A web crawler must remember **500 million** visited URLs with at most a **1% false-positive** rate. Size a Bloom filter: bits per item, total memory, and number of hash functions. Compare with storing the URLs themselves at **60 bytes** each. What does a false positive cost the crawler here?
keyPoints: Total bits ≈ 500M × 9.6 = 4.8 billion bits = 600 MB.
k = 9.6 × 0.693 ≈ 6.6, so 7 hash functions.
Storing URLs: 500M × 60 B = 30 GB, about 50× more.
A false positive means a never-seen URL is wrongly skipped (about 1 in 100 new URLs); no false negatives, so it never re-crawls a seen URL because of the filter.

questions.prompt: Implement a minimal Bloom filter in JavaScript with `add(item)` and `mightContain(item)`, given a helper `hash(str, seed)` that returns a 32-bit unsigned integer. Use `m` bits stored compactly and `k` hash functions. Explain why `mightContain` can return `true` for an item never added, but never `false` for one that was.
questions.hint: Store bits in a `Uint8Array` of `Math.ceil(m / 8)` bytes. Bit `p` lives in byte `p >> 3` at position `p & 7`.
keyPoints: Uses a bit array of size m (e.g. `Uint8Array(Math.ceil(m/8))`) and k hash positions per item (k seeds or double hashing), each `% m`.
`add` sets all k bits; `mightContain` returns true only if all k bits are set.
Correct bit manipulation: `bits[p >> 3] |= 1 << (p & 7)` and test with `&`.
False positives happen because other items may have set all k bits; false negatives cannot happen because bits are never cleared.
Notes deletion is not supported (counting Bloom filters fix that).

questions.prompt: A video site wants to show **unique viewers per video per day** for **10 million videos**. Exact counting stores every viewer ID per video. Estimate the memory for exact sets if popular videos average **5,000** unique viewers with **8-byte** IDs, then propose an approximate approach with its memory and error. Where would a Bloom filter fit, if anywhere?
questions.hint: HyperLogLog in Redis uses 12 KB per counter with about 0.81% standard error, and small counters can be stored more compactly.
keyPoints: Exact: 10M × 5,000 × 8 B = 400 GB per day (more with set overhead), growing with the number of viewers.

HyperLogLog per video: fixed ~12 KB, standard error ≈ 1.04/√16384 ≈ 0.81%; 10M × 12 KB = 120 GB worst case, much less with sparse encoding for small counts (Redis uses a sparse representation for small cardinalities).
Explains HLL intuition: hash viewer IDs, track the max leading-zero run per register, combine with a harmonic mean; duplicates do not change the estimate.
HLLs are mergeable, so daily counters can be combined into weekly/monthly uniques without rescanning.
A Bloom filter answers membership ("has this viewer been counted?") rather than cardinality; it could dedupe per viewer but is not needed with HLL.
